analysis.one_liner: Creates ethics-advice and investigative offices inside the Supreme Court with subpoena power to enforce ethics rules on justices.
analysis.headline: A bill from six Senate Democrats to create ethics-advice and investigative offices for the Supreme Court has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since February 2026 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create two new offices inside the Supreme Court. An Office of Ethics Counsel would advise justices on gifts, financial disclosures, conflicts of interest, recusal, and political activity, and require justices to take ethics training twice a year. An Office of Investigative Counsel would investigate ethics complaints against justices — including conduct involving their spouses and dependents — with the power to issue subpoenas, and would report its findings to the Chief Justice and to congressional committees. Complaints could only be filed by top congressional leaders, not by ordinary citizens.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people gain a way to see whether the nine most powerful judges in the country follow the same ethics rules that apply to other federal officials. Congress's Judiciary and Oversight committees would receive annual reports on the ethics advice justices sought and whether they followed it, plus investigation reports on any misconduct. Taxpayers get a modest, defined cost: a handful of staff attorneys paid at or above $180,000-$225,000 a year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public seeking Supreme Court accountability

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Office of Ethics Counsel to advise justices and their spouses on gifts, financial disclosures, political activity, conflicts of interest, recusal, and leaks of court documents, with the defined terms for what counts as a 'gift' written into law.
Requires every justice to take a training course on these ethics matters twice a year.

Creates an Office of Investigative Counsel that can open formal investigations into justices' conduct — including their spouses' and dependents' conduct — and can compel testimony and documents through subpoenas enforceable in federal court, a tool no current Supreme Court ethics process has.

Requires the ethics office to report to Congress every year on how many times justices sought advice, on which topics, what remedies were recommended, and how often the advice was not followed — creating a public paper trail that does not exist today.
Requires the investigative office to tell the Attorney General whenever it has reasonable grounds to believe a justice violated federal criminal law.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new offices — a chief ethics counsel at no less than $225,000, other counsels at no less than $180,000, and at least three investigative counsels. The justices themselves pay in autonomy: mandatory training, an in-house office tracking their gifts and disclosures, and the possibility of a subpoena-backed investigation. The Chief Justice also gains administrative work, since the offices are appointed by and answer to him.

drawbacks.text: The structure keeps accountability in-house: the Chief Justice appoints the ethics and investigative counsels, can fire them only for cause he judges, and may release or withhold investigation reports to the public 'in his sole discretion' — so meaningful disclosure still depends on the Court's own choices.

Only congressional leaders can file complaints — Judiciary chairs and ranking members, the Senate party leaders, or the House Speaker and Minority Leader. An ordinary citizen who witnesses a justice's misconduct cannot trigger an investigation.

The bill says the Chief Justice is 'authorized to establish' the offices, permissive wording that critics could read as leaving the Court free to decline, even as other sections use mandatory 'shall' language.

Critics argue Congress has no constitutional authority to regulate the Court's internal affairs this way, since the separation of powers makes the judiciary independent of the legislature; the bill includes a severability clause anticipating that parts could be struck down in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give Supreme Court ethics rules real teeth for the first time — subpoena-backed investigations, mandatory training, and annual reporting to Congress — at a trivial dollar cost. But its design quietly hedges: the Chief Justice hires, fires, and can bury the results, and the public can't file complaints. It is a meaningful step toward accountability whose ultimate strength depends on the very officials it polices.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late February 2026 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat ever since with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 25, 2026, joined by five Democratic colleagues: Blumenthal, Hirono, Padilla, Schiff, and Welch.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, which is the standard first stop for a bill.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — as of the latest history.
All six sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, while Republicans control the Senate and its Judiciary Committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supreme Court justices and the Senate majority are better off for now: without committee action, the Court's current ethics regime — self-enforced, with no investigative arm — remains untouched. The public gains nothing until the bill moves or dies.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supreme Court Ethics and Investigations Act and recruited five Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal, Mazie Hirono, Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's five original cosponsors.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Committee received the bill on referral on February 25, 2026, and has taken no action — no hearing or markup has been scheduled.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator has cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee has let it sit without action.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored, while the Senate and its Judiciary Committee are controlled by Republicans who have taken no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill's only concentrated interest is the nine justices themselves, who would face mandatory ethics training, an in-house office logging their gift and disclosure questions, and possible subpoena-backed investigations into their own and their families' conduct. Their institutional interest in self-policing runs directly against the public's interest in outside verification.

The bill creates a small number of senior government attorney positions ($180,000-$225,000+) reserved for outside lawyers with at least 5-7 years of practice experience — a niche but real beneficiary of its passage.

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to advance. Bills referred to Senate committee with no hearing and no cosponsors from the majority party almost never reach the floor, and this Congress ends January 3, 2027. The realistic best case is a committee hearing if Democrats make court ethics a campaign issue; the likely outcome is the bill expiring in committee at the end of the session.
